title: Make the inbox fit a phone
outcome: Build a readable layout that adapts without horizontal scrolling.
story: Amina checks messages on her phone. A page that looks fine on a laptop can still hide content or make buttons too small on a phone.

frames.explanation: A narrow screen needs room for each item.
A media query can change the layout when there is enough space.

sections.title: CSS controls presentation
paragraphs: CSS describes appearance and layout: spacing, colours, sizes, and where elements are placed. A selector chooses which elements receive a rule. For example, .grid chooses elements with class="grid".

Keep the HTML meaning from lesson 8 while changing presentation. A page should remain understandable if its styles fail to load. Use enough contrast and space to make the content readable, rather than depending on decoration to explain the task.

sections.title: Start with the narrow layout
paragraphs: A single column is a useful starting point for a small phone. CSS Grid can arrange the message cards with a consistent gap. grid-template-columns: 1fr makes one column that uses the available space.

Avoid giving the entire page a fixed width such as 900px. A max-width can limit a wide layout while allowing it to shrink. Padding gives the text room at the edges. min-width: 0 lets a grid item shrink instead of forcing the page to overflow.

sections.title: Add a wider-screen rule
paragraphs: A media query applies styles under a condition. @media (min-width: 600px) applies when the preview is at least 600 CSS pixels wide. At that size, two columns can be useful.

The condition is about available layout space, not a particular phone model. Test both sides of the breakpoint. Also test long content and browser zoom: the page should adapt when text needs more room.

sections.title: Make actions comfortable
paragraphs: A button needs enough area to press and a clear focus outline for keyboard use. In this project, give it a minimum height of 44px and readable text. Do not remove the browser’s focus indication without replacing it.
The browser checks inspect the current preview width. Your project evidence should include both a small and a wide view. The course’s browser tests also exercise reference layouts at both widths.

cases.label: Cards use a grid
cases.why: The cards need an explicit layout rule.

cases.label: There is readable space between cards
cases.why: Adjacent cards should not appear as one cramped block.

cases.label: The columns match the current preview width
cases.why: Check the layout on each side of the breakpoint.

cases.label: The page fits the preview
cases.why: Hidden horizontal content makes a phone layout hard to use.

cases.label: The action is large enough to press
cases.why: An action needs a comfortable visible target.

project.title: An inbox for phones and laptops
project.brief: Deliver a message board that remains readable with long content and at different widths. Keep the semantic HTML intact.
deliverables: Small and wide screenshots or a recorded walkthrough.
A short explanation of the breakpoint.

milestones.title: Start small
actions: Use one column and edge padding.

milestones.title: Add space wisely
actions: Use two columns when enough width is available.
Limit the maximum width of long content.

milestones.title: Check awkward content
actions: Try a long message and browser zoom.
Check horizontal scrolling, focus, and button size.

acceptance: A narrow view uses one column.
A wide view uses two columns.
There is no document-level horizontal scroll.
Buttons and focus are comfortable to use.
Long content and zoom are included in the evidence.

tests.expected: Content wraps instead of hiding outside the page.

project.extension: Add an empty-inbox state and check that its spacing remains clear on both layouts.
